You can inspect the exact prompt templates and Zod/JSON schemas inside in the OSSUARY GitHub repository or read the creator's rationale in the DEV Community write-up.Would you like to examine the deterministic Tier 5 template logic that runs when all cloud LLMs fail or explore how the Wikipedia disambiguation filter works in?

28 of 28 messages

That ghost in the machine challenge is done. Complete.

But it led me to a second question.

Gemini web → JSONL?

The conversation I shared above is real, but the parsing — honestly — I fabricated parts of it. The actual raw conversation can be verified here:

👉 https://share.google/aimode/KHPlHfDojASwpXDhG

Open that link. Search for convert conversation to jsonl inside the page.

You will find nothing.

So I asked Gemini itself for help:

A moment please, señor and señorita — Gemini itself cannot do that.

Not from a URL. Not from a share link. Not from anything the user can easily hand it.

If you use any AI, LLM, or agent, please try this and tell me what your machine says:

create jsonl file from link https://share.google/aimode/KHPlHfDojASwpXDhG

I am curious whether every model reports "inaccessible" — or whether some are clever enough to attempt the extraction. Let me know in the comments.

So I built a tool

I did build the tool. It works. Point it at a share link and it produces valid JSONL that DEV.to accepts.

But what use is a tool if this post never surfaces?

So, here is the deal.

If this post finds traction — likes, comments, bookmarks — I will release the tool publicly. Full GitHub repository, documentation, npm package, CLI, browser tool, Chrome extension, and everything I have been polishing.

If it does not — I will keep building it for myself, and release it quietly when the timing is right. No spite. Just honesty: there is little value in publicizing something nobody asked for.

If you would like to test it before launch — reach out on X. I will send you a build.

A small confession

I write to share. But sometimes no one is around.

It feels lonely in the agentic era — surrounded by models that never tire, in front of an audience that rarely responds.

If you have felt this too — building alone, shipping to silence, wondering if anyone out there actually cares — please say hello in the comments. Or on X.

Even a "nice post" means something. It means I am not just talking to the machine.

What is in the tool (a preview)

For the curious, here is the why behind this post:

  1. Extract — parses turn containers from AI Mode HTML while preserving Markdown structure: headings, bold, code blocks, bullet lists.
  2. Scrub — 15 regex patterns for API keys (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, AWS, Slack), JWTs, Sentry DSNs, private keys, emails, home directories, Windows paths, and IPv4. All local — nothing leaves the browser.
  3. Convert — 4 output formats: Claude Code (tested with DEV.to), Codex, GitHub Copilot, Markdown.
  4. Validate and fix — catches the exact issues that cause 0 messages found in DEV.to's parser.

The interesting part is not that it works. It is why it needs to exist. DEV.to's agent-session schema is undocumented. To produce a valid upload, you need the exact structure Claude Code writes to ~/.claude/projects/... — and any deviation (a stray session_meta line, an _title field, assistant content as a string instead of an array) silently fails with 0 messages found.

I reverse-engineered it over one afternoon. Documented it so you never have to.

If it ships, it will include:

  • Browser tool (zero install, all local)
  • CLI with --url (Playwright), --from-console, --interactive, --slice
  • Bookmarklet generator
  • Chrome extension (Manifest V3)
  • GitHub Action
  • .geminiignore for custom scrub patterns
  • Plugin system for ChatGPT, Claude.ai, and future sources
  • --dry-run diff view

For the DEV.to team (feedback while building)

While building the tool, I ran into some rough edges in /agent_sessions/new that I think would save the next developer a few hours. The upload page already lists the six supported tools — that part is clear. The friction was somewhere else.

Context: my source is Google Gemini AI Mode (the web chat at share.google/aimode/...), which is different from Gemini CLI (the local command-line tool that DEV.to already supports). Gemini AI Mode has no native export. So I had to convert my conversation into a valid Claude Code session to get it through the parser. That is a bridge, not a match — and the parser did not make the bridge easy.

Here is what I would genuinely love to see:

1. Error diagnostics that say why it failed

When parsing fails, I get:

0 messages found

But I don't know if that means:

  • Wrong tool selected — file is Claude Code but user picked Codex
  • File malformed — required field is missing
  • File starts with something unexpected — e.g., a session_meta line that isn't real Codex metadata
  • File is a completely different format — user is trying to upload from a tool DEV.to doesn't support yet

Something like:

Parse failed: no valid message lines found.

Detected line types:
  Line 1: type="session_meta" — not supported for Claude Code
  Line 2: type="user" — looks like Claude Code
  Line 3: type="assistant" — looks like Claude Code

Hint: line 1 appears to be from a different format.
Try removing it, or select a different tool from the dropdown.

would have saved me three hours.

2. Distinguish "wrong tool" from "malformed file"

These are very different problems that currently produce the same silent 0 messages found:

  • Wrong tool: user selected Codex but uploaded a Claude Code session
  • Malformed file: correct tool, but a required field is missing

Quick hints in the error panel would help:

  • "File looks like Claude Code — try selecting it from the dropdown."
  • "Expected message.role in line 3. Found: _title."

3. Consider native support for "Gemini AI Mode" (web)

The list currently includes Gemini CLI (the local CLI tool at ~/.gemini/tmp/session-*.json). But Gemini AI Mode — the web chat at share.google/aimode/... — is a distinct use case with no native export.

Adding a parser for AI Mode share links would let thousands of developers share their Gemini web conversations without needing a bridge tool. The fact that I built one is proof of demand.

4. A generic ChatML fallback for unsupported tools

If auto-detection fails, offer a "Upload as generic format" option:

{"role": "user", "content": "..."}
{"role": "assistant", "content": "..."}

Any LLM transcript would work — Gemini AI Mode, Mistral, local models, etc. You would not need to add an extractor for every tool. This single fallback would make the upload page universal.

5. Preview three turns after successful parse

Not as a defensive "catch mistakes early" — as a confirmation that extraction worked as intended. Right now, when a file finally uploads, I still worry: did all turns make it? Is the Markdown intact? A quick preview in the curation UI would answer that in two seconds.

If anyone from the Forem team is reading this, I am happy to open detailed issues or PRs for any of the above. The tool I built is a workaround for one specific gap — but the underlying improvements would help every tool in this space.

One last thing

Here is what I would love from you, dear reader:

  1. Try the prompt above with your favorite LLM. Tell me what it says. I want to build a small museum of "inaccessible" responses.
  2. If you have built alone and felt the silence — comment. Even a single emoji.
  3. If you want to test the tool before I release it — ping me on X.

The ghost is out there, waiting. 🕯️

articles.title: I built a small programming language that runs inside HTML (no eval)
articles.description: Most page interactions are simple: open a menu, switch a tab, check a form. In JavaScript that still...
articles.body_html:
Most page interactions are simple: open a menu, switch a tab, check a form.
In JavaScript that still means selecting elements, adding listeners, and
remembering the DOM API. I wanted to see how short it could be.

So I built Nobelium, a tiny language you write directly in your HTML:

<button id="b">Menu</button>
<ul id="menu" style="display:none"><li>Home</li></ul>

<nobelium>
  when click "#b" {
    toggle "#menu"
  }
</nobelium>

How it works

It isn't a JavaScript framework. It has its own lexer, parser and a
tree-walking interpreter, all written in vanilla JavaScript. It never calls
eval() or Function(), so it works under a strict Content Security Policy.
One script tag, no build step.

What it can do 

let n = saved("visits") or 0
save n + 1 as "visits"
set text "#v" to "you've been here {n + 1} times"

post "/api/items" with { name: "pen" } into item
every 1s { log "tick" }
animate "#box" to { left: 200 } over 600ms

Events, lists and objects, text interpolation, http requests and streaming,
localStorage, timers, animation, tabs and accordions, importing between
files, and a built-in test runner.

Try it

  • Playground (runs the real interpreter): https://nobelium.mcbcode.com/playground
  • Source and docs: https://github.com/xyztoast/nobelium

Honest limits

It's a young project. No lambdas yet, imports need a web server, and it's not
meant to replace JavaScript for real apps. I'd love feedback on the syntax,
especially anything that feels confusing.

articles.title: Japanese Postal Code to Address Auto-Fill, Built From Japan Post's Free Data (No API Key)
articles.description: In Japan, address forms start with the postal code (郵便番号). Users type 7 digits, and the prefecture,...
articles.body_html:
In Japan, address forms start with the postal code (郵便番号). Users type 7 digits, and the prefecture, city and town fill in by themselves. When a form doesn't do this, Japanese users notice right away — it's one of the clearest signs that a checkout "wasn't made for Japan".

I'm a native Japanese developer and I built a checkout plugin for Japanese online stores (Okuricart, free on WordPress.org), so I've written this feature more than once. You don't need a paid API or a third-party script on your checkout page. Japan Post publishes the data for free, and a small build step turns it into static JSON files.

This post covers the data, its quirks, a build script and the front-end code. (For the rest of a Japanese checkout form — name order, furigana, tax-included prices — see my earlier post: How to Build a Checkout Form That Works in Japan.)

1. The data: one CSV from Japan Post

Japan Post publishes the postal code data on its download page. Use the newer UTF-8, one-record-per-line file, utf_ken_all.zip (about 2 MB zipped). It has been published since the June 2023 update.

Why the newer file:

  • It's UTF-8. The classic KEN_ALL.CSV is Shift_JIS.
  • Each postal code is one line. In the classic file, long town names are split across several records, which you have to stitch back together.
  • Readings are full-width katakana (the classic file uses half-width).

About using it: Japan Post's readme says it does not claim copyright on the postal code data and that it may be freely distributed. Still, read the readme yourself before you ship.

The data is updated monthly, with add/delete diff files each month. More on updating at the end.

2. The columns you need

Each line has 15 columns. A row looks roughly like this:

13101,"100","1000001","トウキョウト","チヨダク","チヨダ","東京都","千代田区","千代田",0,0,0,0,0,0

For auto-fill you only need four of them:

# Column Example
3 Postal code (7 digits) 1000001
7 Prefecture 東京都
8 City / ward 千代田区
9 Town 千代田

Columns 4–6 are the readings in katakana (handy if you also want furigana for addresses). Column 13 is a flag that means one postal code covers two or more towns — keep that case in mind, it comes back in section 5.

One more thing: open this file in Excel and the postal codes lose their leading zeros (0600042 becomes 600042). Always treat them as strings.

3. The quirks: town names that aren't town names

The town column isn't always a real town. Japan Post's readme lists a few special values:

  • 以下に掲載がない場合 ("if not listed below") — a catch-all code for the city. It does not identify a town.
  • ○○の次に番地がくる場合 — the block number comes directly after the city name.
  • ○○一円 — the whole municipality, with no town name.

Inserting any of these into a user's address is a bug. Clear them instead.

Town names can also have a note in full-width parentheses, such as 大通西（１～１９丁目） ("Ōdōri-nishi, 1st–19th chōme"). The note describes which block numbers belong to the code; the user types their own block number anyway. Keep the part before （:

const cleanTown = (town) => {
  if (town === '以下に掲載がない場合') return '';
  if (/の次に番地がくる場合$/.test(town)) return '';
  if (/一円$/.test(town)) return '';
  return town.replace(/（.*$/, ''); // "大通西（１～１９丁目）" → "大通西"
};

4. Build step: CSV → small JSON files

More than 100,000 lines is too much to send to every visitor. Split the data by the first three digits of the postal code. The browser then loads only the small file it needs, such as /zip/100.json.

// build-zip.mjs
// Usage: node build-zip.mjs utf_ken_all.csv public/zip
import { readFileSync, mkdirSync, writeFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { join } from 'node:path';

const [, , csvPath, outDir] = process.argv;

const cleanTown = (town) => {
  if (town === '以下に掲載がない場合') return '';
  if (/の次に番地がくる場合$/.test(town)) return '';
  if (/一円$/.test(town)) return '';
  return town.replace(/（.*$/, '');
};

// Fields don't contain ASCII commas, so a plain split is enough here.
// Use a CSV library if you want to be extra safe.
const parseLine = (line) => line.split(',').map((f) => f.replace(/^"|"$/g, ''));

const files = {}; // { "100": { "1000001": [["東京都", "千代田区", "千代田"]] } }

for (const line of readFileSync(csvPath, 'utf8').split(/\r?\n/)) {
  if (!line) continue;
  const c = parseLine(line);
  const zip = c[2];
  const entry = [c[6], c[7], cleanTown(c[8])];
  const bucket = (files[zip.slice(0, 3)] ??= {});
  const list = (bucket[zip] ??= []);
  // After cleaning, two rows can become identical — keep one.
  if (!list.some((e) => e.join() === entry.join())) list.push(entry);
}

mkdirSync(outDir, { recursive: true });
for (const [prefix, data] of Object.entries(files)) {
  writeFileSync(join(outDir, `${prefix}.json`), JSON.stringify(data));
}
console.log(`${Object.keys(files).length} files written to ${outDir}`);

Each postal code maps to a list, because one code can cover several towns. Serve the folder as static files — no server code, no API key.

5. The form: fill in, but don't fight the user

The HTML, with autocomplete attributes so browser autofill still works:

<label>郵便番号 <input name="postal_code" autocomplete="postal-code"
  inputmode="numeric" placeholder="123-4567"></label>

<label>都道府県 <select name="prefecture" autocomplete="address-level1">
  <option value="">選択してください</option>
  <option>北海道</option><option>青森県</option><!-- … all 47 … -->
</select></label>
<label>市区町村 <input name="city" autocomplete="address-level2"></label>
<label>町名 <input name="town"></label>
<label>番地 <input name="address_line1" autocomplete="address-line1"></label>
<label>建物名・部屋番号 <input name="address_line2" autocomplete="address-line2"></label>

(Many Japanese forms put the town at the start of the 番地 field instead of a separate field. Either works — keep it consistent with how you store addresses.)

The script:

const form = document.querySelector('form');

// "〒１００－０００１" → "1000001"  (full-width digits, hyphens, the 〒 mark)
const normalizeZip = (v) => v.normalize('NFKC').replace(/[^0-9]/g, '');

const cache = {};
async function lookup(zip) {
  const key = zip.slice(0, 3);
  cache[key] ??= fetch(`/zip/${key}.json`).then((r) => (r.ok ? r.json() : {}));
  return (await cache[key])[zip] ?? [];
}

// Never overwrite what the user typed themselves.
const edited = new Set();
for (const name of ['prefecture', 'city', 'town']) {
  form.elements[name].addEventListener('input', () => edited.add(name));
}

async function fill() {
  const zip = normalizeZip(form.elements.postal_code.value);
  if (zip.length !== 7) return;

  const hits = await lookup(zip);
  if (hits.length === 0) return; // unknown code: leave the fields alone

  const [prefecture, city, town] = hits[0];
  const set = (name, value) => {
    if (!edited.has(name)) form.elements[name].value = value;
  };
  set('prefecture', prefecture);
  set('city', city);
  // One code, several towns: don't guess.
  set('town', hits.length === 1 ? town : '');

  form.elements.address_line1.focus(); // the user continues with the block number
}

form.elements.postal_code.addEventListener('input', fill);

A few choices worth explaining:

  • Normalize first. Japanese keyboards often type full-width digits (１２３－４５６７). NFKC turns them into 123-4567, then we drop everything that isn't a digit. Don't show an error for full-width input — fix it.
  • Don't guess when there are several towns. If one code covers two or more towns, fill the prefecture and city only, and let the user type the town (or show the choices in a small list).
  • Don't overwrite. If the user has already corrected the city, a late lookup shouldn't put the old value back.
  • Move the cursor to 番地. After the auto-fill, the next thing the user types is the block number.
  • Unknown code = no change. Large businesses and PO boxes have their own postal codes in a separate Japan Post file, so a valid code can be missing from this data. Don't block the form; let the user type the address.

6. Keep it up to date

Postal codes change a little every month (city mergers, new developments, corrections). The simplest approach: re-download utf_ken_all.zip once a month and run the build again. A scheduled CI job works well for this. If you'd rather apply only the changes, Japan Post also publishes monthly add/delete files.

Checklist

  • [ ] Use utf_ken_all.zip (UTF-8, one record per line)
  • [ ] Treat postal codes as strings (leading zeros)
  • [ ] Clear 以下に掲載がない場合 / ○○の次に番地がくる場合 / ○○一円
  • [ ] Cut the （…） note from town names
  • [ ] One code can mean several towns — store a list, don't guess
  • [ ] Normalize input with NFKC; accept hyphens, full-width digits and 〒
  • [ ] Never overwrite fields the user edited; focus 番地 afterwards
  • [ ] Rebuild monthly

Postal-code auto-fill is a small feature, but it's the moment a Japanese user decides whether your form "gets it". The good news: it's an afternoon of work, with no API key and no runtime dependency.

On WooCommerce? If you'd rather not build all of this yourself, my free plugin Okuricart adds furigana fields, postal-code auto-fill (from Japan Post's data), noshi gift-wrap requests and a delivery date picker to both the block and classic checkout.

If you're getting a product ready for Japan, there's a free 31-point checklist (language, names, addresses, checkout, layout and store pages): Free Japan-Ready Checklist. And if you'd like a native Japanese developer to look at your actual screens, I do reviews on Fiverr.

articles.title: Biology's Best Algorithms Aren't Just for Scientists Anymore
articles.description: Ant colonies find short paths without a map, and a slime mold once grew a network about as efficient...
articles.body_html:
Ant colonies find short paths without a map, and a slime mold once grew a network about as efficient as the Tokyo rail system. Honeybee swarms pick a new home by reaching a quorum, with no queen making the call. Researchers have spent decades turning observations like these into equations, testing them, and publishing them through peer review. For most of that time, a small software team could admire the work and do very little with it.

Why small teams couldn't use it

Ant colony optimization has been in the literature since the early 1990s. Reynolds published boids, the flocking model behind a generation of game and film effects, in 1987. Tero and colleagues wrote down the slime mold's network rules in Science in 2010.

Using them was the hard part. You had to:

  • read a paper written for other specialists, in their notation
  • turn the equations into code, often from MATLAB or from nothing
  • build a simulation to see whether your version behaved like theirs
  • figure out which of a dozen parameters actually mattered

That's weeks of work before you learn whether the idea fits your problem. A research lab can spend those weeks. A team of three shipping a product usually can't, so the ideas stayed in the papers.

What changed

A language model can now sit next to you while you read. Paste in the methods section and ask what each symbol means, which parameters the authors swept, and what result they reported. Then have it turn the update rule into a function and build a test harness, a parameter sweep, and a plot around it. Each of those steps used to take days, and now each takes minutes.

Take the pheromone update from Ant System. In the paper it reads:

τij(t+n) = ρ · τij(t) + Δτij, where Δτij = Σk Q / Lk over the ants k that used edge (i, j)

Once every ant has finished a tour, each trail keeps a fraction ρ of its strength and the rest evaporates. Then each ant adds Q / Lk to the edges it used, so shorter tours leave more pheromone. In Rust:

/// One Ant System trail update, run after every ant has finished a tour.
/// `rho` is trail persistence, so 1 - rho evaporates. Each tour is (edges, length).
fn update_pheromone(tau: &mut [Vec<f64>], rho: f64, tours: &[(Vec<(usize, usize)>, f64)], q: f64) {
    for row in tau.iter_mut() {
        for t in row.iter_mut() {
            *t *= rho; // keep rho, lose 1 - rho
        }
    }
    for (edges, length) in tours {
        let deposit = q / length; // Q / L_k: shorter tour, bigger deposit
        for &(i, j) in edges {
            tau[i][j] += deposit;
            tau[j][i] += deposit; // symmetric TSP: (i, j) and (j, i) are one edge
        }
    }
}

You can read the core of a famous algorithm in a minute. The paper still has what took the authors years to learn: why evaporation matters, which values of ρ work, and where the method breaks.

This is why I think small teams are in a good spot right now. Peer review already sorted out which mechanisms hold up, and AI handles the tedious work of getting them into code. What's left for you is the question you care about anyway: does this mechanism help your system?

Reproduce one result before you trust your code

A model can misread an equation as confidently as it reads one correctly, so the workflow needs a check. The paper already gives you one.

  1. Pick one paper and one mechanism.
  2. Have the model extract the update rule, the parameters, and the reported results into a short spec. Check the spec against the equations yourself.
  3. Build the smallest simulation that runs the rule.
  4. Reproduce one figure or number from the paper. That's your acceptance test.
  5. Only then point it at your own problem, and measure it against whatever you do today.

Step 4 is the easiest to skip and the one I'd never skip. If your ants don't find the short path on the paper's benchmark, they won't find it in your system either.

My own experiment: SMESH

I built SMESH this way. The inspiration was mycorrhizal networks, where trees exchange signals through fungal threads in the soil and no single tree is in charge. I wanted AI agents to coordinate the same way. An agent leaves a signal on a shared field, other agents that agree reinforce it, and signals nobody supports fade on their own.

I could run all of it as a plain Rust simulation, with no language model and no API key, and watch the field settle before I trusted it with real agents.

Biologists are still arguing about how much trees really share through those networks. A 2023 review argued the popular "wood wide web" story has gotten ahead of the field evidence. That doesn't hurt the software. I'm borrowing the mechanism, signals that decay unless reinforced, and my simulation tests whether it works for agents, whatever the forest is actually doing.

Where to start

Pick a coordination problem you already have: retries, load balancing, task routing, deciding when a group of services agrees. Then look for the organism that solved something like it.

  • Routing and shortest paths: ant colony optimization, Physarum networks
  • Who does which job: response-threshold models of insect division of labor
  • Group decisions: honeybee quorum sensing
  • Motion and spacing: boids and flocking

Read one paper with a model beside you, reproduce one result, and see whether it earns a place in your system.

What would you borrow first?

articles.title: Git 2.56's history-drop Is 40-77x Faster Than Rebase — I Built It and Got 6x
articles.description: Git 2.56 shipped on September 28 with a new experimental command, git history drop, and the headline...
articles.body_html:
Git 2.56 shipped on September 28 with a new experimental command, git history drop, and the headline number travelling with it is 40 to 77 times faster than rebase. I built Git 2.56 from source this morning, ran the same comparison on my own machine, and got 6 times faster.

Six is not forty. But the story behind the gap is more useful than either number, because the new command's speed is nearly identical on both machines. It's the old way that's wildly different. And that tells you exactly when the new command matters.

Building Git 2.56 first

Git 2.56.0 isn't in Ubuntu's repositories yet, so I built it from the tagged source, the same starting point as the original comparison. It took three tries, and the failures are worth knowing about if you try this yourself.

First failure: curl/curl.h missing. This machine has no libcurl development headers, so the build died on the HTTP code. Second failure: cargo: not found. Git 2.56's default build wants Rust for one of its libraries. Both are fixable without installing anything, because the Makefile has switches for exactly this:

make -j2 NO_CURL=1 NO_RUST=1 prefix=/tmp/git-256 all

Rust is still optional in Git 2.56. The Makefile says so directly, and it stays optional until Git 3.0. The history command itself is plain C, so skipping Rust doesn't remove it. The build took about seven and a half minutes, then tripped at the very last step on msgfmt: not found — a missing translations tool. Cosmetic: the binary was already built, and ./git --version answered git version 2.56.0.

One thing to know before you copy those flags: NO_CURL=1 means this build can't talk HTTP. For this test that doesn't matter: everything happens on local repositories. If you need to clone over HTTPS, build with the headers installed instead.

The comparison, done properly

The original comparison, by Alex Georgiev, published November 13, is a clean piece of work, and I copied its method exactly so the numbers mean something side by side. Fresh repository: one root commit, one target commit to drop, then N descendant commits, each touching a shared file and its own file so the replay has real diff work to do. Clone it bare twice, so both methods start from byte-identical history.

  • Old way: add a linked worktree off the bare repo, run git rebase --onto to skip the target commit, remove the worktree.
  • New way: run git history drop directly against the bare repo. No worktree at all.

Three trials per size. And after every run, I compared the resulting tree hash of main between the two methods. If the trees don't match, the speed means nothing.

My numbers

Descendant commits Rebase (avg of 3) history drop (avg of 3) Speed-up
20 0.193s 0.034s 5.6×
100 0.810s 0.139s 5.8×
400 2.258s 0.325s 6.9×

Every run finished cleanly, and all nine tree comparisons matched exactly. The command does the same work, correctly, in about a sixth of the time.

Now put his numbers next to mine:

Descendant commits His rebase His history drop His speed-up
20 1.418s 0.035s 40.7×
100 7.121s 0.092s 77.5×
400 26.525s 0.362s 73.2×

Look at the right-hand column first. His history-drop times and mine are nearly the same: 0.035s vs 0.034s, 0.092s vs 0.139s, 0.362s vs 0.325s. The new command takes about a third of a second to replay 400 commits, on either machine.

Now look at the rebase column. His rebase took 26.5 seconds for 400 commits. Mine took 2.3. His baseline was ten times slower than mine, and the whole 40–77× headline is made of that difference. The ratio is a property of two machines, not of the command.

Why is his rebase so slow? I can't see his machine, so I won't guess at the cause: disk speed, filesystem, background load, any of those could do it. What I can say is what his own breakdown showed: the worktree setup he suspected was only 26 milliseconds of a 25-second run. The time goes into rebase cherry-picking each commit one at a time, updating the index and the working tree for every single one, even though nobody will ever look at those intermediate states. git history drop never touches a working tree at all — it works on the objects directly. That's the real mechanism, and it holds on my machine too. It just buys you 6× here instead of 70×, because rebase was never that slow here to begin with.

So is the 40–77× claim wrong?

Not wrong. Measured, on his machine, with a published method and matching tree hashes. But it's not a property of the command. If your rebase is already fast, expect single digits. If your rebase is slow — a big repo on a slow disk, hundreds of commits to replay — expect the headline numbers, or better.

The honest way to think about it: git history drop replays 400 commits in about a third of a second, on any machine. Rebase takes however long rebase takes on yours. Measure that, and you'll know your own speed-up.

What else the command does differently

Two things from his write-up are worth carrying over, because they change how you'd use it. Both checked by him directly, not by me.

First, one history drop updates every branch that descends from the dropped commit, not just the one you're standing on. A plain rebase rewrites only your current branch; a second branch past the same commit needs a second rebase. Here, both moved in a single run.

Second, it doesn't run hooks. He put a post-rewrite hook in a test repo and the drop never fired it, while the same hook fired immediately under rebase. If anything in your setup depends on post-rewrite: a notification, a cache update, a linter — switching a script to this command will silently stop that from happening. The man page says hooks aren't run "at the current point in time," which reads like a warning that it may change, not a promise.

And the refusals are clean: dropping the root commit or a merge commit fails immediately with a clear error and leaves nothing behind. A drop that would conflict during replay also fails all-or-nothing. No half-finished state, no conflict markers, no directory to clean up. Compare that with an interactive rebase hitting the same conflict, which stops mid-sequence with a dirty working tree. The man page calls this a design limitation — history rewrites aren't meant to be stateful operations — but from where I'm standing, a command that refuses to start a job it can't finish is a feature.

The catch, stated plainly

The man page marks the whole command experimental: "THIS COMMAND IS EXPERIMENTAL. THE BEHAVIOR MAY CHANGE." It has four subcommands: drop, fixup, reword, split — and I only tested drop. It isn't in any stable release your distribution ships yet, so today it means building from source. And until you've checked your hook dependencies, don't swap it into a script that other people rely on.

But for the job it was built for: dropping a commit from a bare repository, the kind of cleanup you do on a shared repo or a long-lived integration branch — it's the right tool. No throwaway clone, no worktree dance, a third of a second for 400 commits, and the trees come out identical.

My speed-up was 6×. His was 70×. The command was the same. Measure yours.

Sources

  • The claim and the method: Git 2.56's history drop command replays commits 40 to 77 times faster than rebase (Nov 13, 2026) — all of his figures above are his, quoted from that post
  • Git 2.56.0 source: git-2.56.0.tar.gz, mirrors.edge.kernel.org; release date September 28, 2026, per the same post
  • All of my timings, tree hashes and build notes: my own runs this morning, evidence in runs/git-256-history-drop/ (benchmark log, averages, build notes)

articles.title: A Million v7 GUIDs and Half Were Still Out of Order
articles.description: I switched a table to Guid.CreateVersion7() keys for the time-ordering, then benchmarked whether they actually come out sorted. In a tight loop they do not, and here is why.
articles.body_html:
I moved a table's primary key off random GUIDs a little while back. The reason is the usual one: a clustered index hates random inserts. Every new row wants a spot in the middle of the index instead of the end, pages split, the thing fragments, and your inserts get slower the bigger the table gets. Version 7 GUIDs are the tidy fix. They carry a millisecond timestamp in their leading bytes, so new keys sort roughly in creation order and land near the end where the index wants them.

Before I trusted that in production I wanted to see the ordering with my own eyes. So I did the dumbest thing that would show it: generate a pile of keys and count how many came out in order. The answer made me feel a bit silly.

What v7 actually promises

A v7 GUID isn't random all the way down. The first 48 bits are a Unix millisecond timestamp, then a handful of version and variant bits, then the rest is random. Two keys created in different milliseconds sort by those timestamps. That's the whole trick, and it's why people reach for Guid.CreateVersion7() as a key: time-ordered values append instead of scattering.

One thing to pin down first. "Sort order" depends on who's doing the sorting. The UUIDv7 spec and databases like Postgres compare the raw bytes left to right. .NET's own Guid.CompareTo walks the GUID's internal fields instead, which isn't the same thing. So I measured both, because which one you get depends on where the keys end up living.

Here's the byte-order comparer:

static int CompareBytes(Guid a, Guid b)
{
    Span<byte> ba = stackalloc byte[16];
    Span<byte> bb = stackalloc byte[16];
    a.TryWriteBytes(ba, bigEndian: true, out _);
    b.TryWriteBytes(bb, bigEndian: true, out _);
    return ba.SequenceCompareTo(bb);
}

The measurement

I generated a million keys of each kind in a loop and counted adjacent inversions: every spot where a key sorts before the one generated just ahead of it. A perfectly sequential source scores zero. A random source is a coin flip for each pair, so it sits around fifty percent.

static (int inversions, double pct) Inversions(Guid[] g, Comparison<Guid> cmp)
{
    int inv = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i < g.Length; i++)
        if (cmp(g[i], g[i - 1]) < 0) inv++;
    return (inv, 100.0 * inv / (g.Length - 1));
}

I expected v4 near fifty and v7 near zero. I got this:

Out-of-order adjacent pairs (lower = more sequential):
  byte order     v4  50.0%   v7  50.0%
  Guid.CompareTo  v4  50.0%   v7  50.0%

Fifty percent for v7, in plain byte order. The time-ordered key was no more ordered than the random one. Both comparers agreed, which wasn't much comfort.

Why the timestamp didn't help

Millisecond resolution is the catch, and a loop generates keys far faster than one per millisecond. A million of them took around 400 ms on this machine, so roughly a couple thousand keys land in every single tick. I counted how many neighbours shared a millisecond:

v7 keys sharing a millisecond with their neighbour: 999,584 of 999,999 (100.0%)

Every pair. And inside one millisecond, a v7 GUID is just random bits. .NET's implementation doesn't add a monotonic counter to keep same-tick keys in order, so those random tails sort against each other and you're back to a coin flip. The timestamp only breaks ties between milliseconds, and in a tight loop there are almost none of those.

So I slowed down to one key per millisecond, which is a lot closer to how rows actually show up in a real system, and ran it again:

for (int i = 0; i < M; i++)
{
    spread[i] = Guid.CreateVersion7();
    Thread.Sleep(1);
}

v7 spread one-per-ms, 3,000 keys:
  byte order      0.00% out of order
  Guid.CompareTo  0.00% out of order

Zero, under both comparers. Give the timestamp room to move and v7 does exactly what it says on the tin. The ordering was never a lie; it just lives at millisecond resolution, and a benchmark loop runs underneath that.

What I took from it

The practical read is reassuring with one sharp edge. Real inserts are spread across requests over seconds and minutes, so your table gets the append-friendly ordering v7 is sold on, and the fragmentation problem it's meant to solve really does go away. I'm keeping v7 for new tables. But if you ever bulk-generate keys in a loop, seeding a database, running a migration, importing a batch, and expect them to come out sorted, they won't. A few thousand per millisecond is a few thousand coin flips, and the last-mile ordering you were counting on isn't there.

My honest opinion after this: treat the "sequential" label as "sequential at millisecond scale," not "monotonic." Those are different promises. If you genuinely need strictly increasing keys inside a burst, say an outbox you read back in insert order, don't lean on the GUID for it. Add a sequence or a timestamp column and sort on that.

One more caveat worth saying out loud, even though my short spread test didn't trip over it: not every database orders GUIDs by their bytes. SQL Server's uniqueidentifier sorts them in its own way, which has burned people who assumed v7 keys would cluster there the same as in Postgres. Check how your store compares them before you count on the ordering.

Here's the whole thing if you want to run it yourself. It needs the .NET 10 SDK, then dotnet run -c Release:

using System.Diagnostics;

const int N = 1_000_000;

static int CompareBytes(Guid a, Guid b)
{
    Span<byte> ba = stackalloc byte[16];
    Span<byte> bb = stackalloc byte[16];
    a.TryWriteBytes(ba, bigEndian: true, out _);
    b.TryWriteBytes(bb, bigEndian: true, out _);
    return ba.SequenceCompareTo(bb);
}

static (int inversions, double pct) Inversions(Guid[] g, Comparison<Guid> cmp)
{
    int inv = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i < g.Length; i++)
        if (cmp(g[i], g[i - 1]) < 0) inv++;
    return (inv, 100.0 * inv / (g.Length - 1));
}

static Guid[] Generate(int n, Func<Guid> make)
{
    var arr = new Guid[n];
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) arr[i] = make();
    sw.Stop();
    Console.WriteLine($"  generated {n:N0} in {sw.ElapsedMilliseconds,4} ms");
    return arr;
}

Console.WriteLine($"Tight loop, {N:N0} keys each\n");

Console.WriteLine("Guid.NewGuid() (v4, random):");
var v4 = Generate(N, Guid.NewGuid);

Console.WriteLine("Guid.CreateVersion7() (v7, time-ordered):");
var v7 = Generate(N, Guid.CreateVersion7);

Console.WriteLine();

var v4Bytes = Inversions(v4, CompareBytes);
var v7Bytes = Inversions(v7, CompareBytes);
var v4Net = Inversions(v4, (a, b) => a.CompareTo(b));
var v7Net = Inversions(v7, (a, b) => a.CompareTo(b));

Console.WriteLine("Out-of-order adjacent pairs (lower = more sequential):");
Console.WriteLine($"  byte order    v4 {v4Bytes.pct,5:F1}%   v7 {v7Bytes.pct,5:F1}%");
Console.WriteLine($"  Guid.CompareTo v4 {v4Net.pct,5:F1}%   v7 {v7Net.pct,5:F1}%");
Console.WriteLine();

static long SameMsNeighbours(Guid[] g)
{
    long ties = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i < g.Length; i++)
        if (UnixMs(g[i]) == UnixMs(g[i - 1])) ties++;
    return ties;

    static long UnixMs(Guid guid)
    {
        Span<byte> b = stackalloc byte[16];
        guid.TryWriteBytes(b, bigEndian: true, out _);
        long ms = 0;
        for (int k = 0; k < 6; k++) ms = (ms << 8) | b[k];
        return ms;
    }
}

long ties = SameMsNeighbours(v7);
Console.WriteLine($"v7 keys sharing a millisecond with their neighbour: {ties:N0} of {N - 1:N0} ({100.0 * ties / (N - 1):F1}%)");
Console.WriteLine();

const int M = 3_000;
var spread = new Guid[M];
for (int i = 0; i < M; i++)
{
    spread[i] = Guid.CreateVersion7();
    Thread.Sleep(1);
}
var spreadBytes = Inversions(spread, CompareBytes);
var spreadNet = Inversions(spread, (a, b) => a.CompareTo(b));
Console.WriteLine($"v7 spread one-per-ms, {M:N0} keys:");
Console.WriteLine($"  byte order     {spreadBytes.pct,5:F2}% out of order");
Console.WriteLine($"  Guid.CompareTo {spreadNet.pct,5:F2}% out of order");

Have you moved a table to v7 keys yet, or are you still on random GUIDs and a nightly defrag job? Curious whether the fragmentation actually eased up for you.

articles.title: I Sorted Two Million Rows to Keep Ten
articles.description: A leaderboard endpoint that returns ten rows was allocating 56 MB to do it. A bounded PriorityQueue min-heap took it to 568 bytes, with real best-of-five numbers.
articles.body_html:
A leaderboard endpoint I wrote returns the ten highest-scoring players, and for a while I never thought about it twice. Ten rows out, done. Then it started showing up in our gen0 collection graphs during traffic spikes, which made no sense to me, because the response is ten rows. The allocation counter disagreed, and that counter has never once flattered me.

Here's the line that did it, more or less:

var top = players
    .OrderByDescending(p => p.Score)
    .Take(10)
    .ToList();

It reads exactly like what I want. Sort by score, take ten. The problem is the order of operations under the hood. OrderByDescending doesn't know I only want ten until Take shows up later in the chain, so it buffers every player into an internal array first, then sorts enough of it to hand ten back. To return ten rows, it holds all of them at once. On a small table nobody notices. On two million rows it's a very different graph.

Measuring it instead of guessing

I didn't want to argue from a hunch, so I wrote the smallest honest version I could. Two million rows of (id, score), built once up front so the data itself doesn't land on the scorecard. Then the top ten computed two ways, each wrapped in a best-of-five loop with GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() and a checksum so a wrong answer couldn't sneak through.

The LINQ version printed this:

OrderByDescending().Take(K)      56,000,560 bytes    ~43 ms

Fifty-six megabytes to keep ten rows. The number came back byte-for-byte identical on every run, which is what you'd expect from something whose cost is "buffer N, sort N."

Keeping only the ten you care about

The fix is to never hold more than ten rows in the first place. A min-heap capped at K does exactly that: the smallest of the current top ten sits at the root, so any new row only has to beat that root to earn a spot. PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority> has shipped since .NET 6 and it has the one method that makes this clean, EnqueueDequeue, which pushes a new item and pops the smallest in a single rebalance.

var heap = new PriorityQueue<Row, double>(K);
foreach (var r in rows)
{
    if (heap.Count < K)
        heap.Enqueue(r, r.Score);
    else if (r.Score > heap.Peek().Score)
        heap.EnqueueDequeue(r, r.Score);
}

Most rows never make it past the Peek() check. One comparison against the current tenth-best, and they're gone. The heap never grows beyond ten entries, so there's nothing to buffer and nothing for gen0 to clean up afterward. Here's the same two approaches side by side, best-of-five in a cloud container with workstation GC. This isn't a lab, so I care about the ratio, not the absolute milliseconds:

OrderByDescending().Take(K)              56,000,560 bytes    ~43 ms
Bounded PriorityQueue (min-heap of K)           568 bytes     ~6 ms

From fifty-six megabytes to five hundred and sixty-eight bytes, and quicker on the clock on top of it. I'd half expected the time to come out close, since LINQ does partial-sort the top of the buffer rather than sorting all two million. But buffering two million structs and running them through a comparer still costs you, and the heap just... doesn't do that.

When I'd leave the LINQ line alone

Most of the time I'd leave it alone, and I want to be clear about that. If your table has a few thousand rows, fifty-six megabytes becomes a few kilobytes and none of this matters. The LINQ version is shorter, it's obvious to the next person, and obvious code is worth real money. I only reach for the heap when K is tiny next to N and the thing runs hot. The whole win comes from that gap: ten out of two million is enormous leverage, ten out of thirty is nothing. And once K creeps close to N, you're basically sorting anyway, so just sort.

One sharp edge worth knowing: the heap gives you the top ten, but not in sorted order. The root is the smallest of the ten, not the largest. If you need them ranked, drain the heap and reverse, which is cheap because it's only ten items. I forgot that the first time and handed back a leaderboard sorted the wrong way, which is a fun bug to explain.

The full runnable sample

Dropping this in a file and running dotnet run -c Release reproduces the numbers. Tweak N and K at the top to find where the heap stops being worth it.

using System.Diagnostics;

const int N = 2_000_000;
const int K = 10;

var rng = new Random(20261114);
var rows = new Row[N];
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
    rows[i] = new Row(i, rng.NextDouble() * 1000.0);

Console.WriteLine($"N = {N:N0} rows, K = {K}\n");

Measure("OrderByDescending().Take(K)", () =>
{
    var top = rows.OrderByDescending(r => r.Score).Take(K).ToList();
    return Checksum(top);
});

Measure("Bounded PriorityQueue (min-heap of K)", () =>
{
    var heap = new PriorityQueue<Row, double>(K);
    foreach (var r in rows)
    {
        if (heap.Count < K)
            heap.Enqueue(r, r.Score);
        else if (r.Score > heap.Peek().Score)
            heap.EnqueueDequeue(r, r.Score);
    }

    var top = new List<Row>(K);
    while (heap.Count > 0) top.Add(heap.Dequeue());
    top.Reverse();
    return Checksum(top);
});

static double Checksum(List<Row> top)
{
    double sum = 0;
    foreach (var r in top) sum += r.Score;
    return sum;
}

static void Measure(string label, Func<double> run)
{
    run();
    GC.Collect();
    GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers();
    GC.Collect();

    long bestBytes = long.MaxValue;
    double bestMs = double.MaxValue;
    double checksum = 0;

    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
    {
        long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        checksum = run();
        sw.Stop();
        long allocated = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before;

        if (allocated < bestBytes) bestBytes = allocated;
        if (sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds < bestMs) bestMs = sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds;
    }

    Console.WriteLine($"{label,-42} {bestBytes,14:N0} bytes   {bestMs,7:F1} ms   (checksum {checksum:F2})");
}

readonly record struct Row(int Id, double Score);

Have you got a top-N query sitting in a hot path somewhere? Check what it allocates before you assume it's fine. Mine looked harmless for months.

articles.title: The Code I Wrote and No Longer Understand
articles.description: I wrote this file, and I cannot read it.  That is the whole confession. There is no twist coming. The...
articles.body_html:
I wrote this file, and I cannot read it.

That is the whole confession. There is no twist coming. The file is called billing_reconcile.py. It is 214 lines long, and every one of those lines was typed by me, eight months ago, in a week I barely remember. I opened it on a Tuesday morning because a customer had been charged twice for the same order. $63.20, twice. Someone had to find out why. That someone was me. I stared at the first function for eleven minutes. I know it was eleven minutes because I checked the clock twice, the way you check the clock in a waiting room.

The function was called normalize_line_items. I remembered writing the name. I remembered feeling good about the name, the way you feel good about naming a dog. What I did not remember was what it did. It took a list in, gave a list back, and in between it did something with a dictionary, a date, and a variable called temp2. There was a temp2. Which means there was a temp1 somewhere, and I could not find it, and I did not want to know what temp1 had done to earn its number.

My own comments were the worst part. I had left comments. I am the kind of person who leaves comments, and I say that the way people say they floss: proudly, and not entirely truthfully. Above the trickiest block there was a comment that said: "# don't touch this, it works." That was all. No explanation of what "this" was. No explanation of what "works" meant. Just a warning from a stranger who happened to have my name on the commit.

Another one said: "# TODO: fix later (it is later)." I had written that. I had written a joke to myself, eight months ago, and then forgotten the joke and the fix. Past me thought he was funny. Past me was also, apparently, in a hurry.

I should explain the hurry, because the hurry is the whole story, and it is also the excuse I have been rehearsing in case anyone asks.

Eight months ago, we had a deadline. A client was going live on Friday, and the billing page had to stop double-charging people by Thursday, and the fix landed on me on Wednesday afternoon, because I was the only one who had touched that part of the code before. I was. I had touched it. Once. Six months before that. I said yes anyway, because "yes" is the easiest word in the world when someone is standing at your desk.

I wrote the file on Wednesday night, starting at about nine, finishing at about twenty past midnight. I remember the shape of the night better than the code: the music too loud, the coffee gone cold twice, the feeling of going fast. Fast is a drug when you are behind. Every line worked on the first try, or the second, and I did not stop to ask why. I named a variable temp2 because temp1 was taken and I was in no mood to negotiate with myself. I wrote "# don't touch this, it works" at 12:07 a.m., and I meant it as a note to future me, and future me read it eight months later and understood none of it.

The demo went fine. The client went live. The file sat there, working, like a locked room in my own house. I never opened it again. Why would I? It worked. That was the deal I had made with it: it works, I don't touch it. Eight months of peace, bought with one comment.

Then Tuesday morning, the double charge. $63.20, twice. And there I was, standing outside the locked room, holding a key I had made myself, unable to remember which way it turned.

I did what anyone does in that position. I lied, a little, and bought time. I told the team I was going to clean the file up before I fixed it. "Refactor" was the word I used. Refactor is a wonderful word. It sounds like work. It sounds like improvement. It sounds like a man who understands the thing he is about to improve. What I actually did was sit down and re-learn my own code from scratch, the way you would re-learn a language you spoke as a child, one line at a time, with a notebook open beside me.

I started at the top and worked down, writing what each block did in plain words, like a translation. "This part takes the messy list from the payment page." "This part checks the dates." "This part, I think, throws away the duplicates." By noon I had three pages of notebook and a headache. By two o'clock I had found the bug. It was in the part I had marked "don't touch." Of course it was. The duplicate check compared the wrong two things, and it had been comparing the wrong two things for eight months, and the only reason nobody had noticed was that the wrong two things were usually the same. Usually. Not always. Not on Tuesday.

I fixed it in four lines. Four lines, after five hours of reading. I sat there for a while after the fix, looking at the notebook. Five hours of reading, four lines of fix. I decided to think about something else.

The dread, though, was not the bug. The dread was standup the next morning. I could already hear it: "Salam, can you walk us through the billing fix?" And I would have to stand there and walk six people through a file I had only just learned to read, and someone would ask why temp2 was called temp2, and I would have to say "because I was in a hurry at midnight" in front of everyone. I spent the evening drafting my answer in my head, the way you draft a text you never send, and every version sounded worse than the last.

Priya found me at my desk the next morning, still staring at the notebook. Priya sits two desks over. She has been doing this longer than me, and she has the calm of a person who has seen worse. She looked at my notebook — three pages of translation, boxes, arrows, one frustrated doodle of a locked door — and she said, "Yours too?"

"Yours too?" I said.

She told me about her file. It is called email_digests.py. She wrote it a year ago, in a week she describes as "a blur with a deadline in it." She opened it last month and could not follow it. Her comment, the one she remembers, says: "# I don't know why this works and I am afraid to find out." She said it the way you admit you still sleep with the light on sometimes. Not proud. Not ashamed either. Just true.

We sat there for a while, two people who had written code they could no longer read, with coffee going cold on both our desks. Then she said, "I started leaving notes. At the top of every file. For future me. Like a letter." She showed me one, on her phone. It said: "Dear future me, this file sends the weekly email. The weird part in the middle is because Tuesdays are special. Sorry about Tuesdays. — past me."

That evening, I went back to my file and wrote one. At the top, above everything, in plain words:

"Dear future me, this file takes the messy list from the payment page and makes it tidy. The dictionary is the price list. temp2 is the discount. Sorry about temp2. — past me"

I saved the file. Two hundred and fourteen lines, and now the first four were a letter. The stranger and I were on speaking terms again.
