articles.title: I measured my auto video editor on real streams. It was picking the outro.
articles.description: I build Phoenix Editor, a desktop app that takes a long stream or Let's Play recording, cuts the dead...
articles.body_html:
I build Phoenix Editor, a desktop app that takes a long stream or Let's Play recording, cuts the dead air and filler words, and turns the best moments into captioned vertical Shorts. It runs on your own GPU: faster-whisper on NVIDIA, whisper.cpp over Vulkan on AMD and Intel, and the encoder your card has.

For months the test suite ran it against generated fixtures, and everything passed. Then someone called it "vibecoded slop" in public, and I realised I had no evidence they were wrong. Nothing in the repo showed the edits were actually good on real footage.

So I built a harness, ran it on real commentary, and wrote down what came back. This post is the numbers, the bugs they exposed, and the fixes.

The harness

Scoring an edit is harder than it sounds, because "good" is subjective. I picked things I could measure:

  • Words lost. Transcribe the source with a separate model (Whisper medium.en, word timestamps). Any reference word that falls inside a removed range was cut by mistake.
  • Words clipped. A cut boundary that lands inside a word, so the edit says "basi-" and jumps.
  • Fillers removed. Reference "um"s and "uh"s that are actually gone from the render.
  • What the Shorts picker chose, checked by watching them.

The test set was CC-BY and CC-BY-SA videos from archive.org and similar, uploaded by the people who made them:

Length Kind
A raw Twitch stream 3h 09m VTuber overlay, horror RPG
An FPS first-impressions video 20m facecam, lightly edited
A two-player strategy game 11m two voices
Two Let's Play episodes 50m each no commentary at all

The two with no commentary were a free check: the engine should refuse them rather than "edit" a silent video. It did.

Round one

3h stream FPS strategy
Removed 63 of 189 min 5.7 of 20 min 2.3 of 11 min
Reference words lost 4.1% 1.8% 2.5%
Words with a cut inside them 2.6% 1.7% 2.4%
Fillers removed 2 of 19 2 of 36 3 of 8

Losing one word in 25 sounds small until you watch it. Every lost word came from a silence cut. About 60% sat within 0.4 s of a cut edge, so the padding was too tight. The rest were deep inside a "silence" that wasn't: quiet speech under game audio.

The fillers were worse, and the cause was not my code. Whisper doesn't write "um" and "uh" by default. It cleans them out of the transcript, and a filler detector that reads the transcript can't cut what isn't there.

And the Shorts were bad enough to be funny:

  • On the 3-hour stream, all five Shorts came from the first eight minutes: pre-game chat about having a cold. None from the two boss fights the stream was named after.
  • On the FPS video, three of five were the outro.
  • On the strategy video, the intro and the outro.

Why the Shorts picker failed

The first version scored fixed 15-second windows on a 5-second grid by loudness and words per second. That rewards exactly the wrong thing. When does a streamer talk fast and loud? When they're explaining something to the camera: the intro, the outro, the sponsor bit. When something actually happens in the game, they react: "oh", "no no no", "wait", "let's go". Short bursts, not monologue.

And a grid window starts and ends wherever the grid says, which is mid-sentence.

The fixes

Cut edges. Silence cuts now stop short of every transcribed word: 80 ms before it, 120 ms after. One subtle bug on the way: there's a cap on how long a silence cut can be, and it was judged after carving out words. A quiet half hour with one word in it got chopped into dozens of jump cuts, removing 504 s instead of 171. The cap is now judged on the whole pause first.

Fillers. Whisper can be told to write them: hotwords on faster-whisper, an initial prompt on whisper.cpp. That worked, with a catch: primed to hear "uh", it also hears some short real words as "uh". Measured against the reference transcript, the culprits were the low-confidence ones and the implausibly long ones (a 3-second "uh" is a stretched timestamp over real speech). So a filler is only cut when Whisper is at least 40% sure and it's at most 1.2 s long. Leaving an "um" in is cheaper than cutting a word.

There was a second filler bug, and it's my favourite: the fillers that were detected mostly never left the render. The pause padding, scene snapping and word guards that protect speech were also erasing the tiny filler cuts. Only 6 of 27 detected fillers made it out. Filler cuts now skip those steps and keep a 40 ms margin.

Repetition loops. Turning on hotwords together with conditioning on previous text locked faster-whisper into repeating one line from minute 70 of the 3-hour stream to the end: 386 words where there should have been about 1,500. Conditioning is off now, and both backends collapse runs of four or more identical sentences.

Shorts, rebuilt:

  1. Clips are built from whole sentences, 20 to 45 seconds, so a Short opens on a thought and closes on one.
  2. The main signal is reaction density, not talk. Loudness and speech rate only count relative to the speaker's own level a few minutes either side, so someone who is loud all night doesn't win everywhere.
  3. A vision pass labels scenes. Combat and cutscenes add to a clip; menus, loading screens and idle subtract.
  4. Intros, outros and "links in the description" are ruled out, and the first and last couple of minutes of a long recording are discounted.
  5. Picks are spread out, with a minimum gap that scales with the recording's length. And if there aren't five good moments, you get fewer Shorts rather than filler.

The layout changed too. On a facecam recording, the old reframer followed the face, so the 9:16 crop was the webcam corner and the gameplay was cropped away. Now the facecam is found (YuNet plus edge refinement) and stacked above the gameplay, with 2 to 3 word captions at the seam.

Round two

FPS before FPS after strategy before strategy after
Reference words lost 1.8% 0.99% 2.5% 0.22%
Words with a cut inside them 1.7% 1.36% 2.4% 1.25%
Fillers removed from the render ~2 20 of 27 detected ~3 3 of 5 detected

The Shorts on the FPS video are now five gameplay reactions ("whoa whoa whoa", "it feels like a war zone", "just ate a grenade"). The strategy video gets four mid-game moments.

What's still weak

The raw 3-hour VTuber stream. The avatar has no face to stack, the vision pass mislabels an intermission card as gameplay, and some of the transcribed speech is game dialogue rather than the streamer. Those picks are still poor, and I'd rather say so than pretend.

The filler confidence gate also only works on the NVIDIA path for now, because whisper.cpp's per-word confidence isn't wired in yet.

What I'd tell anyone building something similar

  • Test on real footage early. Generated fixtures tested that the code ran. They couldn't tell me it picked the outro.
  • Score against an independent transcript. If you score your edit with the same transcript you used to make it, every mistake is invisible.
  • Whisper's defaults are tuned for clean text, not editing. If you need disfluencies, ask for them, then filter what comes back.
  • "Loud and fast" is not "exciting". Reactions are.

Phoenix Editor runs on Windows and Linux, on AMD or NVIDIA, and nothing uploads. There's a 7-day free trial with every feature and no watermark, and a setup guide if you want to throw a VOD at it. If it picks your outro, tell me.

articles.title: Body Radar: a game where you guess your breath and pulse before the camera does
articles.description: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge           What I Built   Body Radar...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge

What I Built

Body Radar is a desktop game about how well you know your own body. You guess first, then a webcam shows you what it measured.

Round 1 is a 30-second breath tap. You look away from the screen and press Space at the top of each inhale. Afterward a ring replays your taps in magenta against the inhale peaks the camera found in blue, and tells you how many you caught and whether you tend to tap early or late. Round 2 asks you to guess your pulse with a slider. You lock it in, and the camera shows what it measured.

A small robot called Pip sits beside the ring and reacts to how you did. The game runs in Electron on the Presage SmartSpectra SDK. It gives no medical readings.

Code

Github URL

The README has the full setup. You need Node.js 20 or newer and a SmartSpectra API key:

npm install
SMARTSPECTRA_API_KEY=your_key npm start

For Practice mode, run npm run build:renderer once and open renderer/index.html in a browser.

How It Responds to Human Signals

Two Presage signals drive the game. Round 1 uses the breathing trace (breathing.upperTrace) and Round 2 uses pulse rate (cardio.pulseRate). The SDK's validation status runs alongside both and tells the app when the signal is poor. The app also requests the breathing rate metric, which the game does not show yet.

The camera is read live during a round, and the game hides the result on purpose until you have committed. In Round 1 the trace arrives while you tap, and the ring replays it when the 30 seconds end. In Round 2 a progress bar fills as each stable pulse reading arrives. The app waits for at least 8 readings (no sooner than 8 seconds, no later than 60), drops the first quarter while the estimate settles, and takes the median. If the SDK reports a problem such as too little light or too much motion, the status chip changes right away and Pip's caption says what to fix.

How I integrated the SDK:

  1. The SDK runs in the Electron renderer. Its renderer entry is CommonJS, so I bundle it with esbuild.
  2. The setup screen opens the preview with getUserMedia and hands the same stream to the SDK with useMediaStream. Only one camera stream is open, and you can see it.
  3. The SDK is created with the three metrics I use and with telemetry off: 
sdk = new SmartSpectraSDK({
  apiKey: config.apiKey,
  requestedMetrics: [MetricType.CHEST_BREATHING, MetricType.BREATHING_RATE, MetricType.PULSE_RATE],
  enableTelemetry: false,
});
sdk.useMediaStream(stream);
await sdk.start();
  1. metrics events go through decodeMetrics. Breathing trace timestamps arrive in microseconds, and I map them onto the wall clock so your taps and the peaks share one timeline. Pulse readings count only when the SDK marks them stable.
  2. validationStatus codes map to short hints such as "Too dark. Turn toward a light."
  3. When the window closes, the app stops and destroys the SDK and releases the camera stream.

A few things went wrong on the way. The SDK takes integer MetricType codes, and my first version passed strings. It also ran the SDK in the main process while the preview opened the same camera again, so two things competed for one device. Moving the SDK into the renderer with a shared stream fixed that. My first setup check looked for skin color to find a face, which could block people with darker skin or tinted lighting, so I replaced it with a check on brightness and movement and let the SDK report face position. And a fixed 10-second pulse timer was too short for some people, which is why Round 2 now waits for stable readings.

Prize Categories

I'm entering Most Creative or Delightful Use.

Most body-sensing demos show you a number. I wanted to ask what you think first, because the gap between your guess and the measurement is where the game happens. You see it on a single ring, with your magenta taps next to the blue peaks the camera found.

Pip makes it friendlier to be wrong. The app has light and dark themes and reduced-motion support, and it uses the Atkinson Hyperlegible font. Round 1 plays from the keyboard with Space.

Consent and Data Handling

  • Consent: the opening screen explains what the app reads before anything starts. The camera turns on when you press Turn on preview, and the SDK begins processing only after you press Start camera. The preview stays in the window the whole time, and only the app's own page is allowed to use the camera.
  • Storage: none. There are no files, accounts, database or analytics. Results live in memory until you close the window.
  • Sharing: Body Radar sends no video or results anywhere. The SmartSpectra SDK contacts Presage to check the API key.
  • SDK telemetry: off (enableTelemetry: false). Per the SDK docs, telemetry never includes video frames or vital signs.
  • Retention and deletion: the app keeps nothing, and closing the window clears the results.
  • AI services: none.
  • The API key is read from an environment variable and held in memory.
  • Where the SDK processes video frames: I make no claim about that. Presage's SDK documentation covers it.

Body Radar makes no diagnosis, suggests no treatment and supports no medical decision. It runs only when you start it, and the camera preview is always visible while it does.

Agent Session

I used AI coding assistants for parts of this build, mostly to review my code against the SDK's typings and to draft fixes that I then tested on my own camera.

articles.title: Preventing Feedback Loops in a Two-Way Vue Unit Converter
articles.description: If both fields in a Vue unit converter are editable, how do you stop a calculated result from...
articles.body_html:
If both fields in a Vue unit converter are editable, how do you stop a calculated result from overwriting the user's input? I use explicit conversion directions and synchronous watchers so that each numeric edit updates the opposite field without bouncing back.

A Vue length converter gave me a compact example. Each side can update the other, both results are rounded, and a swap button changes units and values together. The arithmetic is routine; the interesting part is stopping intermediate state from becoming a new user instruction.

One Conversion Function, Two Directions

The component imports a shared length-unit table and conversion helper. Each unit has a scale relative to meters, so a conversion goes from the source unit to meters and then from meters to the destination unit.

That keeps the component out of the business of maintaining a separate formula for every possible pair. With eight units, separate directional formulas would create many opportunities for a mismatched constant. A shared base-unit representation needs one scale per unit instead.

The component aliases the shared conversion and rounding helpers, then uses them in two mirror-image synchronization functions:

function syncFromLeft() {
  if (isSyncing) return;
  isSyncing = true;
  toValue.value = roundResult(convert(fromValue.value, fromUnit.value, toUnit.value));
  isSyncing = false;
}

function syncFromRight() {
  if (isSyncing) return;
  isSyncing = true;
  fromValue.value = roundResult(convert(toValue.value, toUnit.value, fromUnit.value));
  isSyncing = false;
}

The direction is explicit. Editing the left side means the right side is derived; editing the right side means the left side is derived. The implementation does not average the fields or try to reconcile both as independent measurements.

There is an important boundary to that rule: changing either unit dropdown always recalculates from the left. The component does not store a "last edited side." After entering 1 inch on the right, the left reads 2.54 centimeters. Changing the right unit to feet keeps that left value and produces 0.083333 feet; it does not reinterpret the right-hand 1 as one foot.

The isSyncing variable is not rendered state. It is an imperative guard around a short synchronous operation. Making it a ref would not help explain the calculation, because the template has no reason to react to it.

The Guard Depends on Watcher Timing

Here are the value watchers:

watch(fromValue, syncFromLeft, { flush: "sync" });
watch(toValue, syncFromRight, { flush: "sync" });

The flush mode is part of the design, not an incidental performance setting.

When syncFromLeft writes toValue, the synchronous watcher for the right side runs while isSyncing is still true. Its guard returns immediately. The original left-side value remains the authoritative input.

Without that coordination, a rounded result could be converted back and overwrite the user's original value. Vue may stop some repeated assignments when the primitive value is unchanged, so this is not a claim that every naive converter must loop forever. The more subtle problem is that derived output becomes a new input, potentially losing precision.

For a concrete trace, entering 1 centimeter produces 0.393701 inches after rounding. Converting that displayed result back produces 1.000001 centimeters. The right-side watcher must return before performing that second conversion; otherwise the original 1 is no longer preserved. This is worth testing even when the form appears to settle without an infinite loop.

Using default queued watchers with the same short-lived boolean would change the reasoning. A callback that runs after the original function releases the guard no longer sees the protected state. If you change watcher scheduling, you need to reconsider the guard rather than assuming it still protects the same operation.

Synchronous watchers are not batched, so this is a deliberate trade-off for two small calculations, not a blanket recommendation for large reactive collections.

The converter is synchronous, with no request or awaited task inside either helper. I would not copy this pattern unchanged into an asynchronous address lookup or pricing form. A boolean released before an asynchronous response arrives does not solve response ordering or stale updates.

Swap Units and Values as One State Change

The swap button has a related problem: assignments happen one at a time, but the operation conceptually changes four values together.

function swapUnits() {
  isSyncing = true;
  const tmpUnit = fromUnit.value;
  const tmpVal = fromValue.value;
  fromUnit.value = toUnit.value;
  toUnit.value = tmpUnit;
  fromValue.value = toValue.value;
  toValue.value = tmpVal;
  isSyncing = false;
  persistUnits();
}

Without the guard, changing the first unit could immediately trigger a calculation using one new unit and one old unit. A later assignment might then swap a value that has already been recalculated from that temporary combination.

The guarded version snapshots the original left unit and value, exchanges the pairs, and only then releases synchronization. It preserves the currently displayed relationship instead of inventing an intermediate conversion.

This is not a general Vue transaction: the assignments still happen separately. The boolean only tells these synchronization functions to ignore intermediate states. Another synchronous watcher would need its own coordination if it depended on the complete pair.

The unit watchers also use synchronous flushing. They call the left-to-right synchronization function and persist unit choices only when the guard is not active. The swap function explicitly persists once after completing the exchange.

That persistence stores the selected unit keys, not the entered measurement. On mount, saved units are loaded if their keys exist in the unit map. The initial values remain deterministic for server rendering, and an initial synchronization already runs during setup so the first rendered result is not just a placeholder zero.

I like this separation: rendering a valid default conversion, restoring preferences, and processing a user edit are distinct operations. They should not depend on a single late initialization step.

Rounding and Validation Still Need Honest Boundaries

The shared helper rounds ordinary finite results to six decimal places, not six significant figures:

function roundLengthResult(v) {
  if (!isFinite(v)) return 0;
  return Math.round(v * 1e6) / 1e6;
}

Returning a number avoids padding the display with trailing zeros. It does not preserve arbitrary measurement precision or guarantee a reversible round trip. For example, 0.1 millimeters is 0.0000001 kilometers, which rounds to zero here. A fixed number of decimal places has very different consequences depending on the destination unit.

Swapping the displayed pair preserves the displayed values. It cannot recover digits already removed when a previous conversion was rounded. Likewise, entering a rounded result on the opposite side makes that rounded number the new source of truth.

The shared conversion function also coerces values with Number(value) || 0. Empty or nonnumeric input can therefore produce zero rather than a distinct invalid result. Clearing the left input leaves that source field empty while calculating zero on the right; the guard prevents the derived zero from being written back into the empty field. The numeric inputs have no min restriction, and the helper accepts negative numbers. I would not advertise these fields as a complete domain-validation layer. If an application requires a positive physical length or a separate invalid state, those would be additional rules, not behavior this converter already provides.

Useful tests include editing each side, changing either unit, swapping after editing the right side, and swapping twice. The important assertions concern both numbers and units. Checking only that a familiar conversion appears once would miss the state-transition bugs this design is meant to prevent.

I turned this two-way synchronization example into a small free tool: Length Unit Converter.

articles.title: What it took to add Jalali dates to form-js
articles.description: I was working on a project that needed a form builder for the forms inside business processes. After...
articles.body_html:
I was working on a project that needed a form builder for the forms inside business processes. After some research, I found that BPMN-IO's form-js was a good library for it, but it lacked something our users needed. They work in Persian, so the forms needed the Jalali calendar in the date logic as well as on screen, in the form viewer and in the form builder, and form-js only knows Gregorian dates. Forking the library was ruled out from the start, because a fork of a project this size becomes a second product that you maintain alone.

I already knew the calendar. Most of the work was fitting it into form-js's architecture: a large monorepo I hadn't written, code that is hard to follow, and very little documentation for the internals I needed to change. Before I could change anything safely, I had to work out how it fitted together. Below is the map I ended up with, and what the feature needed from each part of it.

The code has moved on since I worked on it. I've checked the details below against the current source.

How form-js is put together

form-js is a monorepo of separately published packages:

  • form-js-viewer renders a form from a JSON schema and data, validates it and produces the submission.
  • form-js-editor is the drag-and-drop form builder. It depends on the viewer.
  • form-js-playground combines the two with panels for input and output data, and depends on both.
  • form-json-schema describes what a valid form schema is.
  • form-js bundles the viewer, editor and playground. Today there is also an i18n package for translations and an integration test package.

Nothing in it is wired together by hand. Each package is assembled from dependency-injection modules (didi, the same container the rest of bpmn.io uses), and almost every behaviour is a service you can replace. The viewer's core module alone registers the event bus, the importer, the field factory, a field registry and a field-instance registry, a path registry, the layouter and the validator. Features such as the FEEL expression language, templating, markdown, viewer commands and repeating groups are further modules on top.

Fields are Preact components. A FormFields registry maps each field type (textfield, number, datetime and the rest) to its component, and the renderer looks components up there by type.

The editor is a second application on the same pieces. It builds its own injector with modeling and a command stack, a properties panel, drag and drop, a palette and selection. Its EditorFormFields extends the viewer's registry and swaps in editor versions of a handful of field types:

export class EditorFormFields extends FormFields {
  constructor() {
    super();
    editorFormFields.forEach((formField) => {
      this.register(formField.config.type, formField);
    });
  }
}

The date field isn't one of those, so the builder's canvas renders the viewer's own date component inside a different injector.

How a value moves through it

A value goes through five stages, and the date feature had to hold at every one of them:

  1. Import: importSchema hands the schema to the importer, which creates every field, registers it, and claims its key or path in the path registry.
  2. Initial data: Each field's value is read from the supplied data at its value path, falls back to its default, and passes through the field type's sanitizeValue. For the date field, that's where an incoming string becomes a value the component accepts, or gets discarded.
  3. Changes: A component reports a new value. The form updates its state and emits field.updated and changed on the event bus, and anything listening reacts.
  4. Expressions and validation: Conditions, templates and some validation bounds (min, max and length limits) are FEEL expressions evaluated against the current data, and the validator runs on every relevant change.
  5. Submit: The submission collects every keyed, enabled field instance by its value path, which may be nested, from the current state.

So the value in state is a contract. Expressions read it, the validator reads it, the submission sends it on, and the process engine on the other side stores it. For dates that contract is an ISO string, YYYY-MM-DD, with separate formats for time and date-time.

Inside the date field

Inside the date field, a single value passes through four libraries and conventions:

  • The picker wraps flatpickr, whose calendar is Gregorian.
  • The value is written as an ISO string by Luxon.
  • The display format is derived from Intl, based on the browser's locale.
  • Validation helpers check the string's shape by splitting it on - and T.

That has a consequence that is easy to miss. In a fa-IR browser, Intl defaults to the Persian calendar:

new Intl.DateTimeFormat("fa-IR").resolvedOptions().calendar;
// "persian"

The field takes its date pattern from there, and flatpickr then fills that pattern with Gregorian values. Out of the box, the format and the value come from two different calendars.

What the feature needed

The design decision that everything else followed from was to keep the stored value exactly as it was: Gregorian, ISO, the same contract as before. Jalali lives at the edges, in what a person sees, picks and types. That kept FEEL conditions, validation, the submission and every system downstream unchanged, and it kept existing forms and saved data valid.

Getting there meant reaching every layer above:

  • The viewer needed a Jalali date field. flatpickr only knows the Gregorian calendar, so the new field uses jalaliDatePicker instead, a small picker with no dependencies that handles Jalali dates and times. The harder part was that the two libraries disagree about who owns the input. form-js renders it as a Preact component and treats its value as state. jalaliDatePicker attaches itself to inputs on focus, writes Jalali strings such as 1403/01/10 into them and announces the change with its own jdp:change event. The field sits between the two. It opens the picker on its own input, listens for the picker's events, converts the Jalali string to the ISO value the form expects and back again on every render, and parses dates people type by hand. The time and date-time subtypes map onto the picker's time options. The field is registered under the existing datetime type through a module, so the registry resolves to it and every schema that already used the field picked it up.
  • Existing ISO values and defaults had to come through the import and sanitising path into the new field unchanged, for the date, time and date-time subtypes, and conversions had to happen at the right time zone, so a value near midnight in Tehran stays on the right day.
  • Users type Persian or Arabic digits, such as ۱۴۰۵, and the stock number field accepts a key only if it matches /^[0-9]$/. Input had to be normalised before it reached any of that logic.
  • Bounds such as "no dates in the past" are evaluated on the Gregorian value. The picker has its own minDate and maxDate, so they had to be fed from the same field settings, or the calendar would offer days the validator then rejects. The messages still had to make sense in Jalali.
  • The editor has its own injector and its own field registry, so the field had to be registered there too, so the builder's canvas shows the same field a user will see. The properties panel has its own date-time settings and constraints, which also had to read correctly.
  • The playground, where the editor and viewer meet, had to work as well. It is the one place where the round trip from schema to rendered form to submitted data can be tested.
  • jalaliDatePicker attaches its calendar to the page body by default, outside the form's own markup. In the builder that meant it had to stack above the canvas and the properties panel instead of opening behind them, and it had to be styled to match the form instead of the about 50 lines of flatpickr styling the stock field relies on.

Every one of these sits outside the library's source, as modules registered through its extension points and a stylesheet layer of our own, so upgrades stayed routine and we never had to fork.

Working in a codebase like that

Most of my time went into finding out where things happen. Code that runs through dependency injection and an event bus doesn't let you follow a call from one place to the next. A service is resolved by name, an event is emitted in one package and handled in another, and the documentation stops where the public API does.

What worked for me was following a single value end to end, from the schema through import, state, the event bus, validation and submission, and writing down what I found. Those notes became the documentation I needed. The rule I would apply to any library this size is to change nothing until you can say where your change will be resolved, rendered, validated and serialised.

What I would do differently

I would ask earlier whether this was the right foundation. form-js is a capable library, and it was much larger than our requirements. Every feature we added had to fit someone else's architecture, which cost time in every sprint. Building our own form layer would have cost more in the first month and less in every month after.

Originally published on mamrez.com. I'm a senior frontend engineer working in React and TypeScript, open to remote roles and to relocating within Europe. My CV and contact details are at https://mamrez.com/cv/.

articles.title: A same-word game that runs in the browser: state, scoring, and the tie problem
articles.description: Two players join a room, get the seed word "moon", and type a word each in secret. If both write...
articles.body_html:
Two players join a room, get the seed word "moon", and type a word each in secret. If both write "night", they score. If one writes "night" and the other writes "star", the round ends with nothing, even though both answers are perfectly good associations.

That gap is the whole game. I built SameWord, a word-association game for two to four players that runs in a browser tab with no account and no install. The interesting part was never comparing two strings. It was deciding what a round is, how a round is won, and what happens when the room does not agree.

Here are the three parts that took the most thought.

A round has one state, and everyone shares it

A game is five rounds. Each round has the same shape: the server picks a seed word, every player submits exactly one word, then everything is revealed at once.

The reveal is the only moment anything is shared. Before that, the room shows a counter like "2 of 3" and nothing else. Nobody can see which words are in, so nobody can copy an answer. When the last player submits, or the clock hits zero, the words appear together with the name attached to each.

Two timers have to agree for that to work: the round clock (30 or 60 seconds, chosen when the room is created) and the reveal. The round clock is the authoritative one. If it hits zero with someone still typing, the round is scored on the words that arrived; an empty slot is skipped rather than filled with a placeholder. That rule matters in practice, because a four-player room with a 60-second clock will almost never have everyone submit early.

The host presses Start on each round, which creates an obvious failure mode: a distracted host freezes the room. The reveal advances on its own 20 seconds after it appears, so the game keeps moving even if nobody clicks.

Two ways to win, and no partial credit

A round scores when one of two things is true.

A match: every submitted word is the same word. The comparison trims spaces and ignores capital letters, so "MOON" and " moon " are the same. Plurals are not. "rabbit" and "rabbits" are different answers, and so are "ocean" and "sea", because the game cannot score a synonym as a match on its own.

The second path is the same-meaning confirm. The words differ, but every online player taps a button saying they treat the words as one answer. Then the round counts.

That button exists because word matching fails exactly where language is interesting. Plural forms, synonyms, and typos are all things a room can agree on and a string comparison cannot. But a confirm that any one player could trigger would be a free point, so it needs unanimity.

There is no partial credit. A round is a win or it is not, and the result screen counts wins out of five. Players who want a finer signal have asked for per-round closeness scores; I left them out because "you were sort of close" turns a five-round game into a spreadsheet.

The tie problem is the default, not the edge case

The seed for round two comes from round one. After a win, the next seed is the word the room agreed on. After a no-match round, the next seed is the word that appeared most often.

That rule has a hole, and the hole is the normal path whenever two people play.

In a two-player room with no match, the two words appear once each. The frequency is 1 to 1 every single time, so "most frequent" never picks a winner. Three players can produce a three-way tie; four players tie two and two quite often. A tie-breaker is not a rare branch in this game, it is the road most rounds take.

The rule I settled on: when words are tied on frequency, the word that was submitted first becomes the seed. It is deterministic, it needs no extra round, and every client can compute it from the same reveal data.

The cost is real. Submission order is a function of typing speed and network latency, so in a two-player game the next seed is often decided by who was faster rather than by anything about the words. A player who types immediately after the seed appears gets to steer the following round. I considered three alternatives. A random pick from the tied words is fairer but makes the game feel arbitrary. Replaying the round punishes everyone for a tie. Carrying the previous seed forward breaks the chain that gives round two its context.

None of those were clearly better, so the fast-finger rule stays. If I were starting over, I would show the tie resolution on screen instead of resolving it silently. Players already suspect the seed is not random; telling them the rule is cheaper than letting them guess.

Unanimity breaks before anything else does

The same-meaning confirm asks every online player. With two people that is two taps and a small cost. With four it is the most fragile part of the game, because one player who does not tap turns a round everyone else agreed on into a no-match.

"Online player" is doing quiet work in that sentence. Someone who closed the tab cannot confirm, so they cannot block a round either. Someone who is still connected but walking away can. The rules put no timer on the confirm, so a four-player room can stall on a decision that three people already made.

I have not solved that one. A majority rule would make the four-player mode feel fairer, but it would also let two players outvote the third, and the entire game is built on the idea that the room is the unit, not the individual.

What a browser-only room actually costs

No accounts means the room code is the only shared object: six characters generated when the room is created, copied into whatever chat the group already uses. There is nothing to install and nothing to sign up for, and the host's player list is the only social proof that anyone is there.

The constraint shows up in small places. Words are capped at 24 characters and limited to letters, spaces, hyphens and apostrophes, which keeps the comparison simple and stops the input from becoming a message box. The one-phone mode exists for the same reason: two people, one device, hand it over between turns, words stay hidden until the reveal.

None of this is exotic. A five-round game with a room code and a countdown is about as small as a multiplayer browser game gets. The state machine, the unanimity rule, and the tie-breaker are where the game actually lives, and all three are decisions about what the room is allowed to disagree on.

SameWord is free at playsameword.com, and the rules are written up at playsameword.com/how-to-play.

articles.title: Loading a 72 MB JSON list on a TV box without running out of memory
articles.description: I make a media player for Android TV boxes, phones and Windows. People sign in with the playlist...
articles.body_html:
I make a media player for Android TV boxes, phones and Windows. People sign in with the playlist their provider gives them, and the app downloads three lists from the provider's server: live channels, films and series. Each one is a single JSON array.

On paper that is easy: await (await fetch(url)).json(). In practice it broke on real hardware, and the fix taught me more about memory on cheap devices than anything else this year.

How big these lists really are

These are measured numbers from real accounts, not guesses:

  • one list alone: 72 MB of JSON
  • the three lists of one account together: 156 MB
  • another account: 28,445 channels, 157,163 films and 50,149 series, 131 MB in total

Reading one of those whole needs several times its size in memory at the same moment: the raw bytes, the string made from them, and every object JSON.parse builds. On an Android TV box with 4 GB of RAM the download simply failed. The fetch threw "Network request failed", our app showed "No internet connection", and the playlist stayed empty. The user's internet was fine. The box had run out of room.

Rule one: never hold the list

The fix was to stop treating the response as one value.

  1. Stream the body. The list is read as the bytes arrive, a piece at a time.
  2. Cut the array, don't parse it. A small splitter walks only the outline of the array: brackets, braces and strings. When it has one complete item it hands that item's text to JSON.parse on its own. A 72 MB list becomes tens of thousands of tiny parses.
  3. Back-pressure. The splitter hands items over 2,000 at a time and reads no further until the database has taken them. Memory stays flat no matter how long the list is.
  4. Save in fixed blocks. Rows go into SQLite through one prepared INSERT of 2,900 rows that is built once and reused. Leftover rows wait for the next batch, so every statement is the same shape.

The trap: backslashes

The first version of the splitter was fast on one server and painfully slow on another, with lists of the same size.

PHP writes every / as \/, so lists from PHP panels are full of escapes. The splitter looked for the next backslash inside each string to know whether a quote was escaped. On a list written as plain JSON there are no backslashes at all, so every search ran to the end of the piece. In Node, 150,000 films (50 MB) took 0.15 s in PHP's format and 6 s as plain JSON, and minutes when the pieces were 1 MB.

The fix: remember where the next backslash is and search again only after you pass it. Same for the next quote. Now both formats take about 0.1 s, and the time grows only with the size of the list, not with what is inside it.

A related case: PHP writes every non-ASCII letter as \uXXXX. 20,000 test series with Arabic plots (72 MB) took 3.6 s before that change and 0.5 s after.

On Android: a file beats the network stream

Streaming fixed the crashes, but the box was still slow. The timers showed the cost was turning many small network pieces (8 KB each) into text on the JavaScript thread.

So on Android the list now goes to a file in the cache folder first, written by native code, and is read back one megabyte at a time. A megabyte is in memory, never the list. Text that arrives in large runs is also text the engine parses quickly: JSON.parse of a 78 MB film list took 0.55 s in megabyte runs, against 4 s when the same runs were put together from 8 KB pieces.

On one list of 200,000 films that meant about 4 s to read back, parse, build rows and save, where the same work took about 12 s before. If the device has less than 300 MB free, or the file cannot be written, the app falls back to reading the list as it arrives.

What I would tell anyone loading big JSON on a TV box

  • Measure on the device. My PC was never the problem.
  • Treat "Network request failed" with suspicion on low-memory hardware. It may be memory, not network.
  • Never response.json() something whose size you don't control.
  • Keep batches a fixed size so statements can be prepared once.
  • Test with the ugliest real data you can get: escaped slashes, \u escapes, huge single items.

If you want to see the result, the app is NewTV Player. It is a player only, with no content of its own: you add the playlist from your provider. I'm its developer, so take the plug for what it is; the techniques above work in any React Native app.

This post was drafted by an AI assistant from my own project notes and measurements.

articles.title: Intl.DateTimeFormat Gotchas When Showing a City's Local Time
articles.description: I was wiring a small world clock: given one instant, show the wall time in New York, London, and...
articles.body_html:
I was wiring a small world clock: given one instant, show the wall time in New York, London, and Seoul. Intl.DateTimeFormat is the right API for this — you pass an IANA time zone and a locale, and the runtime does the offset and DST math. The surprises sit in the options that look obvious: timeZone: "EST", timeZoneName: "short", and hour12 next to hourCycle.

Every snippet below was run on Node.js v24.22.1 (ICU 78.3, CLDR 48, tzdb 2026e). The process default time zone on this machine is Asia/Seoul.

Date#getHours() is the host's hour, not the city's

A Date stores an instant (milliseconds since the Unix epoch). getHours(), getDate(), and toString() convert that instant in the runtime zone. They will not give you New York's clock just because you are thinking about New York.

const instant = new Date("2026-11-14T12:00:00Z"); // noon UTC

console.log(instant.getHours());     // 21  (Seoul, UTC+9)
console.log(instant.getUTCHours());  // 12
console.log(instant.toString());
// Sat Nov 14 2026 21:00:00 GMT+0900 (Korean Standard Time)

const fmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", {
  timeZone: "America/New_York",
  hour: "numeric",
  minute: "2-digit",
  timeZoneName: "short",
});
console.log(fmt.format(instant)); // 7:00 AM EST

If you omit timeZone, the formatter uses the same default as Date.prototype.toString() — here, Asia/Seoul. Always pass the city zone you mean.

"EST" is not Eastern Time. In tzdb it is Panama.

This is the bug that looks right in November and wrong in July. Pass timeZone: "EST" and you might assume you will get US Eastern Time, with daylight saving in the summer. You will not.

On this runtime, EST canonicalizes to America/Panama. Panama has been on UTC−5 without DST for a long time, and IANA's backward file links the old System V name EST there. MST is the same class of footgun: it links to America/Phoenix (Arizona, no DST), not America/Denver.

const summer = new Date("2026-07-14T16:00:00Z");

for (const timeZone of ["EST", "America/New_York", "MST", "America/Denver"]) {
  const fmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", {
    timeZone,
    month: "short",
    day: "numeric",
    hour: "numeric",
    minute: "2-digit",
    hourCycle: "h23",
    timeZoneName: "shortOffset",
  });
  console.log(timeZone, fmt.resolvedOptions().timeZone, fmt.format(summer));
}

EST               America/Panama    Jul 14, 11:00 GMT-5
America/New_York  America/New_York  Jul 14, 12:00 GMT-4
MST               America/Phoenix   Jul 14, 09:00 GMT-7
America/Denver    America/Denver    Jul 14, 10:00 GMT-6

At that instant New York is on EDT (UTC−4). The EST formatter is still on UTC−5, so it is an hour behind the city you thought you asked for. resolvedOptions().timeZone is how you see the alias the runtime actually used.

Three more naming traps:

  • Abbreviations are not unique identifiers. IANA's own guidance is not to use them that way — in English-speaking North America "CST" is US Central Standard Time; in China it is China Standard Time.
  • Some abbreviations just throw. KST and EDT are a RangeError: Invalid time zone specified on this Node build.
  • Etc/GMT+5 is not UTC+5. The IANA etcetera file keeps POSIX signs, which count positive offsets west of Greenwich, so Etc/GMT+5 is UTC−5. The same noon-UTC instant formats as 07:00 GMT-5.

Use a city identifier from the tz database: America/New_York, America/Denver, Asia/Seoul. Offset-only IDs like "-05:00" are valid in Intl, but they do not follow DST.

timeZoneName: "short" is a localized label, not a stable code

Even after you pass a real IANA zone, timeZoneName: "short" is not a reliable ticker. It is a localized string, and the exact text is implementation- and locale-dependent. Formatting noon UTC on 2026-11-14 in America/New_York:

Locale short shortOffset shortGeneric
en-US EST GMT-5 ET
en-GB GMT-5 GMT-5 New York Time
fr-FR UTC−5 UTC−5 heure : New York
ko-KR GMT-5 GMT-5 뉴욕 시간

en-GB does not print EST. fr-FR uses UTC and a minus sign (U+2212), not GMT-5. en-US has no short abbreviation for Asia/Seoul — the same options print 9:00 PM GMT+9, not KST. In July, Europe/London at 2026-07-14T16:00:00Z is 5:00 PM GMT+1 in en-US but 17:00 BST in en-GB.

MDN notes that time zone display may fall back to another format when a preferred string is unavailable. That is why shortGeneric in en-GB becomes New York Time rather than ET.

If you are building a world clock and you want the offset to be comparable across locales, prefer timeZoneName: "shortOffset" or "longOffset", and pull the label out with formatToParts() instead of scraping the formatted string.

hour12 silently wins, and midnight has four spellings

ECMA-402 defines four hour cycles: h11 and h23 run 0–11 and 0–23; h12 and h24 run 1–12 and 1–24. The difference is obvious at local midnight and noon. For America/New_York on 2026-11-14T05:00:00Z (midnight) and 2026-11-14T17:00:00Z (noon):

        midnight                  noon
h11     Sat, Nov 14, 00:00 AM     Sat, Nov 14, 00:00 PM
h12     Sat, Nov 14, 12:00 AM     Sat, Nov 14, 12:00 PM
h23     Sat, Nov 14, 00:00        Sat, Nov 14, 12:00
h24     Sat, Nov 14, 24:00        Sat, Nov 14, 12:00

h24 keeps the calendar date and prints 24:00. That is what the spec says to do with hour 0; it does not roll the date back to November 13.

If you also pass hour12, it overrides hourCycle. MDN is explicit, and the runtime agrees:

const fmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", {
  timeZone: "America/New_York",
  hour: "numeric",
  minute: "2-digit",
  hourCycle: "h23",
  hour12: true,
});
console.log(fmt.resolvedOptions().hourCycle); // h12
console.log(fmt.format(new Date("2026-11-14T05:00:00Z"))); // 12:00 AM

The locale decides which 12-hour cycle you get. hour12: true on en-US becomes h12 (12:00 AM). On ja-JP it becomes h11 (午前0:00). Locale defaults without either option also differ: en-US and ko-KR use h12; en-GB and ja-JP use h23.

If you care about the cycle, set hourCycle and leave hour12 unset.

Don't parse format(), and don't Number() Arabic digits

format() is a display string. Field order, separators, calendar, and digits all follow the locale:

en-US  11/14/2026, 07:00
en-GB  14/11/2026, 07:00
ko-KR  2026. 11. 14. 07:00
th-TH  14/11/2569 07:00           // Buddhist calendar (year 2569)
ar-EG  ١٤/١١/٢٠٢٦، ٠٧:٠٠         // Arabic-Indic digits

Number("07") is 7. Number("٠٧") is NaN. th-TH will happily hand you a year you can add to, except it is 543 years ahead of the Gregorian year.

formatToParts() gives you named fields. If those fields are going into arithmetic — sorting rows, computing an offset — pin calendar: "gregory" and numberingSystem: "latn" so the values are ASCII digits in the Gregorian calendar. Leave the user's locale for the string you actually render.

dateStyle / timeStyle cannot be combined with individual options such as hour or timeZoneName — that is a TypeError. Ask for the style or the parts, not both.

A helper that returns numbers, not a sentence

Here is the pattern I ended up with for "what is the wall clock in this city?":

function cityWallTime(date, timeZone) {
  const fmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", {
    timeZone,
    weekday: "short",
    year: "numeric",
    month: "2-digit",
    day: "2-digit",
    hour: "2-digit",
    minute: "2-digit",
    second: "2-digit",
    hourCycle: "h23",
    timeZoneName: "shortOffset",
    calendar: "gregory",
    numberingSystem: "latn",
  });

  const parts = Object.fromEntries(
    fmt.formatToParts(date)
      .filter((p) => p.type !== "literal")
      .map((p) => [p.type, p.value]),
  );

  const asUTC = Date.UTC(
    Number(parts.year),
    Number(parts.month) - 1,
    Number(parts.day),
    Number(parts.hour),
    Number(parts.minute),
    Number(parts.second),
  );

  return {
    timeZone,
    weekday: parts.weekday,
    year: Number(parts.year),
    month: Number(parts.month),
    day: Number(parts.day),
    hour: Number(parts.hour),
    minute: Number(parts.minute),
    second: Number(parts.second),
    timeZoneName: parts.timeZoneName,
    offsetMinutes: (asUTC - date.getTime()) / 60_000,
  };
}

const instant = new Date("2026-11-14T12:00:00Z");
console.log(cityWallTime(instant, "America/New_York"));
console.log(cityWallTime(instant, "Europe/London"));
console.log(cityWallTime(instant, "Asia/Seoul"));
console.log(cityWallTime(instant, "Pacific/Auckland"));

America/New_York  Sat 2026-11-14 07:00:00  GMT-5  offsetMinutes: -300
Europe/London     Sat 2026-11-14 12:00:00  GMT+0   offsetMinutes: 0
Asia/Seoul        Sat 2026-11-14 21:00:00  GMT+9   offsetMinutes: 540
Pacific/Auckland  Sun 2026-11-15 01:00:00  GMT+13  offsetMinutes: 780

Auckland is already Sunday. That is the whole reason to do this with a named zone and parts, not with getHours() and a hardcoded offset.

The offset trick is: format the instant in the city, then interpret those civil fields as if they were UTC. The millisecond difference is the offset. It also holds for half-hour and 45-minute zones: Asia/Kolkata is 330 minutes year-round here, and Pacific/Chatham is 765 minutes on 2026-07-14 and 825 on 2026-11-14.

Checklist

  1. Always pass a tzdb city identifier (America/New_York), never EST / MST / KST.
  2. Log resolvedOptions().timeZone. Aliases are real: this Node build reports Asia/Calcutta when you pass Asia/Kolkata.
  3. Prefer timeZoneName: "shortOffset" when the offset is the thing the user needs to compare.
  4. Set hourCycle explicitly, and do not also set hour12 if you care which cycle you get.
  5. Use formatToParts() for structure. Pin calendar: "gregory" and numberingSystem: "latn" when the values have to be numbers.
  6. Store UTC instants (or offset-aware strings). Format at the edge.

I ran into these while building a small city-to-city converter, WorldTimeSync: https://time.wooooju.com/en/

Sources

  • MDN: Intl.DateTimeFormat() constructor (hour12 overrides hourCycle; timeZoneName values and fallback)
  • MDN: formatToParts()
  • MDN: resolvedOptions()
  • ECMA-402 (hour cycles; h24 maps hour 0 to 24)
  • IANA tzdb backward (EST → America/Panama, MST → America/Phoenix)
  • IANA tzdb etcetera (POSIX sign on Etc/GMT±N)
  • IANA: Time zone and daylight saving time data (abbreviations are not unique identifiers)
